los.text: Describe the importance of pain management and palliative care in clinical settings
los.html:
• Pain is common and often undertreated: about two-thirds of people with advanced cancer have significant pain
    • untreated pain worsens sleep, mood, mobility, recovery (e.g. post-operative chest infections, DVT) and trust.
  • Palliative care (WHO): improves the quality of life of patients and families facing life-threatening illness, by early identification, assessment and treatment of pain and other physical, psychosocial and spiritual problems.
    • It neither hastens nor postpones death.
  • Total pain (Cicely Saunders): physical, psychological, social and spiritual distress all contribute to the pain a patient reports.
  • Good pain control and palliative care are core skills for every doctor, not only specialists: most end-of-life care is given by GPs and hospital teams.

los.text: Identify the indications, mechanisms and side effects of analgesic drugs.
los.html:
Drug (step)MechanismKey side effects / cautions
Paracetamol (step 1)Central COX inhibition (exact mechanism unclear)Hepatotoxic in overdose; max 4 g/day (reduce if <50 kg, liver disease, alcohol)
NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) (step 1)COX-1/COX-2 inhibition → fewer prostaglandinsGI bleeding (give a PPI), AKI, fluid retention, asthma, CV risk; avoid in CKD, heart failure, peptic ulcer
Codeine (step 2)Prodrug: CYP2D6 → morphineConstipation; poor or ultra-rapid metabolisers; not for under-12s
Tramadol (step 2)Weak μ agonist + serotonin/noradrenaline reuptake inhibitionSeizures, serotonin syndrome (with SSRIs), confusion
Morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl (step 3)μ-opioid receptor agonists: inhibit transmission in the dorsal horn, activate descending inhibitionConstipation (always co-prescribe a laxative), nausea, drowsiness, confusion, itch, respiratory depression; accumulate in renal failure (morphine)
Neuropathic agentsAmitriptyline/duloxetine (boost descending inhibition); gabapentin/pregabalin (α2δ calcium-channel subunit)Drowsiness, dizziness, dependence (gabapentinoids are Schedule 3 CDs); TCA anticholinergic effects
AdjuvantsDexamethasone (oedema around tumour), bisphosphonates (bone pain), hyoscine butylbromide (colic), local anaesthetics (Na⁺ channel block)
WHO analgesic ladder
  • Non-opioid → weak opioid → strong opioid, ± adjuvants at every step
  • Give regularly ("by the clock"), by mouth where possible, with breakthrough doses.
Opioid toxicity
  • Drowsiness, confusion, hallucinations, myoclonus, pinpoint pupils, slow breathing.
  • Reverse life-threatening respiratory depression with naloxone (titrated in palliative patients, so pain control isn't lost).

los.text: Describe the assessment of acute, persistent and palliative pain in various clinical settings
sessions: Assessment of pain: acute, persistent, palliative
los.html:
TypeDefinitionAssessment focus
AcuteRecent onset, linked to injury/surgery/illness, expected to resolveSOCRATES, pain score, cause, red flags, response to analgesia
Persistent (chronic)>3 monthsImpact on function, sleep, mood, work; beliefs and fears (yellow flags); previous treatments; medication use and dependence
PalliativeIn progressive life-limiting illnessEach pain separately (patients often have several), mechanism (bone, nerve, visceral, colic), total pain
ToolsNumerical rating scale (0–10), visual analogue scale, faces scale (children), Abbey pain scale or PAINAD (dementia, non-verbal patients).
Nociceptive vs neuropathicNeuropathic pain is burning, shooting, electric, with numbness, allodynia (pain from light touch) and dermatomal or nerve distribution (screen with DN4 or LANSS).

los.text: Describe the role of palliative care and when it is appropriate
los.html:
Role
  • Symptom control
  • Psychological and spiritual support
  • Help with decisions and advance care planning
  • Support for families and carers (including bereavement)
  • Coordinating care across settings.
When
  • From diagnosis of any life-limiting illness, alongside disease-modifying treatment, not only in the last days
  • Not just cancer (heart failure, COPD, dementia, MND, end-stage kidney and liver disease, frailty).
Triggers
  • The "surprise question" ("Would I be surprised if this patient died in the next 12 months?")
  • Repeated admissions
  • Declining function
  • Uncontrolled symptoms
  • Patient request.
  • Gold Standards Framework registers in primary care.
Levels
  • Generalist palliative care (GPs, district nurses, ward teams) for most
  • Specialist palliative care (hospice, hospital and community specialist teams) for complex physical, psychological or family problems.

los.text: Link the anatomical structures, biochemical process, control mechanism of the nociceptive pathways to their clinical signs, symptoms and treatment.
los.html:
StageWhat happensTreatment link
TransductionTissue damage releases prostaglandins, bradykinin, H⁺, K⁺, substance P; nociceptors (free nerve endings) fireNSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis
Transmission
  • Aδ fibres (fast, sharp, well localised) and C fibres (slow, dull, burning) → dorsal horn (laminae I, II = substantia gelatinosa, V)
  • Glutamate and substance P
Local anaesthetics block Na⁺ channels; opioids act pre- and post-synaptically in the dorsal horn; gabapentinoids reduce Ca²⁺ influx
Ascending pathwaysSpinothalamic tract decussates within 1–2 segments → thalamus (VPL) → somatosensory cortex (location); spinoreticular → limbic system (emotion)Explains crossed sensory loss in cord lesions
Modulation
  • Gate control: Aβ (touch) fibres activate inhibitory interneurons (rubbing, TENS)
  • Descending inhibition from the periaqueductal grey → rostral ventromedial medulla → dorsal horn using serotonin, noradrenaline, endogenous opioids
TCAs/SNRIs strengthen descending inhibition; opioids act at the PAG
PerceptionCortex and limbic system: mood, attention and beliefs change painPsychological therapies
SensitisationPeripheral (inflammatory mediators lower nociceptor thresholds: hyperalgesia) and central ("wind-up" via NMDA receptors: allodynia, spreading pain) → why ketamine (NMDA antagonist) helps some resistant pain.
Referred painVisceral and somatic afferents converge on the same dorsal horn neurons (e.g. MI → left arm; diaphragm → shoulder tip).

los.text: Describe the management of acute, persistent and palliative pain in various clinical settings
sessions: Specific treatment: acute, persistent, palliative pain
los.html:
SettingManagement
Acute (e.g. post-operative, injury)
  • Multimodal: regular paracetamol ± NSAID, opioid for moderate–severe pain (immediate-release, short course, with laxative and antiemetic), regional anaesthesia (nerve blocks, epidural), PCA
  • Treat the cause
  • Reassess pain scores
  • Step down quickly
Persistent primary pain (NICE NG193)
  • Exercise, psychological therapy (CBT, ACT), acupuncture
  • An antidepressant (amitriptyline, duloxetine, SSRIs) may be considered.
  • Don't start paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, gabapentinoids or benzodiazepines
Persistent secondary painTreat the cause (e.g. OA: exercise, weight loss, topical NSAIDs)
Neuropathic (NICE CG173)
  • Amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin first line (switch if ineffective)
  • Carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia
  • Capsaicin cream for localised pain
  • Tramadol only as short-term rescue
Palliative
  • WHO ladder titrated to effect
  • Regular strong opioid + breakthrough doses
  • Adjuvants matched to the pain type
  • Non-drug measures (radiotherapy for bone metastases, nerve blocks)
  • Opioids in persistent non-cancer pain give little long-term benefit
    • harm rises sharply above ~120 mg/day oral morphine equivalent without extra benefit (Faculty of Pain Medicine, "Opioids Aware"): taper if not helping.

los.text: Describe the assessment and management of pain in palliative care
los.html:
• Assess each pain: site, mechanism, pattern (constant, incident pain on movement, end-of-dose), effect of current analgesia, total pain.
Pain typeCluesTreatment
Bone (metastases)Localised tenderness, worse on weight-bearingNSAID, opioid, single-fraction radiotherapy, bisphosphonate/denosumab; check calcium; consider fracture or MSCC
Neuropathic (nerve compression or infiltration)Burning, shooting, numbnessAdjuvants (amitriptyline, gabapentinoid), dexamethasone, opioid, nerve block
Liver capsuleRUQ ache, hepatomegalyDexamethasone, NSAID
Raised ICPMorning headache, vomitingDexamethasone
Bowel colicCramping (obstruction)Hyoscine butylbromide; stop stimulant laxatives and prokinetics
Starting a strong opioid(NICE CG140)
  • Oral morphine, e.g. 20–30 mg/day in total (MR 10–15 mg twice daily, or IR 5 mg 4-hourly) plus IR morphine 5 mg PRN for breakthrough
  • Always prescribe a laxative
  • Antiemetic available.
  • Titrate daily by the breakthrough doses used.
Breakthrough dose1/10 to 1/6 of the total 24-hour dose.
Renal impairment(eGFR <30)Morphine metabolites accumulate → use oxycodone at low dose, or alfentanil/fentanyl; seek specialist advice.

los.text: Describe the role of holistic care in palliation
los.html:
• Holistic care treats the person
    • not just the disease: physical (symptoms, function)
    • psychological (fear, anxiety, depression)
    • social (carers, finances, housing, benefits such as the special rules for terminal illness)
    • spiritual (meaning, faith, legacy, unfinished business).
  • Family and carers are part of the unit of care: information, respite, practical help, bereavement support.
  • MDT: GP, palliative care nurse specialists (CNS), district nurses, hospice, OT and physio (equipment, mobility), dietitian, social worker, chaplaincy, psychology, pharmacist.
  • Tools: holistic needs assessment, IPOS (Integrated Palliative care Outcome Scale), "What matters to you?"

los.text: Describe the role and importance of advanced care planning in clinical care
los.html:
• Advance care planning (ACP): a voluntary process of discussion
    • while the person has capacity
    • about their values
    • wishes and preferences for future care
    • in case they later can't decide or communicate.
OutputLegal status
Statement of wishes and preferences (e.g. preferred place of care and death)Not legally binding, but must be considered in best interests decisions
Advance decision to refuse treatment (ADRT)
  • Legally binding if valid and applicable
  • For life-sustaining treatment it must be written, signed, witnessed and state "even if my life is at risk" (MCA 2005)
Lasting power of attorney (health and welfare)Appointed attorney can make decisions when the person lacks capacity (life-sustaining treatment only if expressly authorised)
DNACPR decision
  • A clinical decision
  • Must be discussed with the patient (or family) unless it would cause physical or psychological harm
  • Recorded on the regional form
  • Why it matters: care matches what the patient wants, fewer unwanted admissions and treatments, less distress for families, better use of resources.
    • Share it (GP record, out-of-hours, ambulance) and review it as things change.
  • ReSPECT forms record recommendations for emergency care and treatment (used in parts of the UK).

los.text: Describe the assessment and management of symptoms other than pain in palliative care
los.html:
SymptomManagement
Nausea and vomiting (choose by cause)
  • Chemical/metabolic (opioids, hypercalcaemia, renal failure): haloperidol
  • Gastric stasis: metoclopramide (avoid in complete bowel obstruction)
  • Raised ICP, vestibular, bowel obstruction: cyclizine
  • Chemotherapy: ondansetron ± dexamethasone
  • Broad spectrum second line: levomepromazine
ConstipationVery common (opioids, immobility): stimulant + softener (senna + docusate) or macrogol; rectal measures; methylnaltrexone for resistant opioid-induced constipation
Breathlessness
  • Treat the cause (effusion, anaemia, infection)
  • Fan, positioning, breathing techniques
  • Low-dose oral morphine
  • Benzodiazepine (e.g. lorazepam sublingual) for panic
  • Oxygen only if hypoxic
Respiratory secretions (last days)Reposition; hyoscine butylbromide or glycopyrronium SC
Agitation / deliriumLook for causes (pain, retention, constipation, drugs, hypercalcaemia); haloperidol; terminal agitation: midazolam
Anorexia, fatigue, mouth problemsSmall meals, steroids short term, mouth care (candida: nystatin/fluconazole)
  • Palliative emergencies: hypercalcaemia (confusion, constipation, thirst: IV fluids + IV bisphosphonate)
    • metastatic spinal cord compression (back pain, weakness: dexamethasone 16 mg, MRI whole spine within 24 h, radiotherapy/surgery)
    • SVC obstruction (dexamethasone, stent)
    • catastrophic bleed (dark towels, midazolam, stay with the patient)
    • neutropenic sepsis.

los.text: Describe the importance of a range of services in care of a patient's last days
sessions: Care in the last days of life
los.html:
Recognising dying(NICE NG31)Increasing weakness and sleepiness, bedbound, reduced intake, difficulty swallowing tablets, changes in breathing (Cheyne–Stokes, noisy secretions), cool mottled peripheries, reduced consciousness.
Care in the last days
  • Discuss with the patient and family
  • Individualised care plan
  • Stop non-essential medicines and observations
  • Support oral intake and mouth care (consider clinically assisted hydration case by case)
  • Anticipatory ("just in case") medicines prescribed SC for:
SymptomTypical drug
Pain / breathlessnessMorphine (or oxycodone/alfentanil in renal failure)
NauseaLevomepromazine or haloperidol
AgitationMidazolam
SecretionsHyoscine butylbromide (or glycopyrronium)
  • Syringe driver if regular SC drugs are needed.
  • Services: GP and district nurses (24/7 community nursing)
    • specialist palliative care teams
    • hospices (inpatient, day, hospice at home)
    • Marie Curie night sitting
    • out-of-hours services (shared ACP and DNACPR)
    • social care and fast-track NHS continuing healthcare funding
    • chaplaincy
    • pharmacy
    • bereavement support
    • after death: verification, medical examiner and death certification.

los.text: Describe the assessment and management of persistent pain in various clinical settings
los.html:
Assessment
  • Pain >3 months
  • Biopsychosocial history: pain story
  • Function
  • Sleep
  • Mood (PHQ-9)
  • Beliefs and fears (yellow flags: belief that pain means harm, fear-avoidance, catastrophising, low mood, work problems, compensation claims)
  • Previous treatments
  • Analgesic and alcohol use
  • Examination and red flags to exclude serious disease
  • Tools: Brief Pain Inventory, STarT Back (back pain risk stratification).
Management
  • Explain pain (nervous system sensitisation, "hurt doesn't equal harm"); set functional goals rather than "zero pain".
  • Physical activity and exercise, physiotherapy, pacing.
  • Psychological: CBT, ACT, pain management programmes (MDT).
  • Drugs: limited role; review and taper ineffective opioids and gabapentinoids; antidepressants for some.
  • Interventions for selected causes (e.g. radiofrequency denervation for facet joint pain).
  • Address sleep, mood, work and social support.

los.text: Conduct a comprehensive, patient-centred assessment in end-of-life care, addressing physical, emotional, social, and spiritual needs
los.html:
DomainAsk about / assess
PhysicalPain, breathlessness, nausea, constipation, fatigue, appetite, mouth, skin, mobility, continence, sleep
EmotionalFear, anxiety, low mood, anger, understanding of the illness
SocialWho's at home, carers' coping, finances, housing, dependants, practical needs (equipment, care packages)
SpiritualWhat gives meaning, faith and rituals, worries about dying, legacy, unresolved relationships
WishesWhat matters most, preferred place of care and death, ACP, organ/tissue donation
  • Patient-centred: ask permission
    • go at their pace ("How much do you want to know?")
    • use open questions and ICE
    • involve family if the patient wishes
    • use tools such as IPOS or holistic needs assessment
    • document and share with the team.

los.text: Identify and understand the key processes involved in end-of-life care planning, including advanced care planning and decision-making
los.html:
• Key processes:
1Recognise that someone may be in the last year (or days) of life (surprise question, decline, frailty).
2. Assess capacity(Mental Capacity Act 2005)Presume capacity; can they understand, retain, weigh and communicate the decision?
3. Advance care planningWishes and preferences, ADRT, LPA for health and welfare, preferred place of death.
4. Treatment escalation and DNACPR decisions
  • a senior clinical decision
  • Discuss with the patient
  • If they lack capacity, consult the LPA or family (they inform but don't decide unless an LPA).
5Best interests decisions if the person lacks capacity and has no valid ADRT or LPA (consider their past wishes; IMCA if nobody else).
6Anticipatory medicines, equipment, care package, fast-track funding.
7. Communicate and shareGP, out-of-hours, ambulance, care home; regular review.

los.text: Communicate with sensitivity and empathy, addressing complex emotional and ethical issues in end-of-life care discussions with patients and their families
los.html:
FrameworksSPIKES for bad news; ask–tell–ask; NURSE for emotions (Name, Understand, Respect, Support, Explore).
Skills
  • Warning shot
  • Plain words ("dying", "died": avoid euphemisms)
  • Silence
  • Empathy
  • Check understanding
  • Honest answers about prognosis (ranges: "days to short weeks")
  • Balance realism with hope (what can still be achieved)
  • Don't promise what you can't deliver.
Difficult situationApproach
Family asks you not to tell the patient (collusion)Explore their fears; explain the patient's right to information; ask the patient what they want to know; don't lie
Request for futile treatment
  • Explore what they hope it will achieve
  • Explain why it won't help
  • Doctors needn't give treatment that isn't clinically indicated
  • Offer a second opinion
Request to hasten death
  • Explore the reasons (pain, fear, burden)
  • Address symptoms and distress
  • Assisting suicide is a criminal offence (Suicide Act 1961)
  • Proposed changes to the law are being debated, so check the current position
Conflict within the familyMeet together, focus on the patient's wishes, MDT and senior support
  • Look after yourself and colleagues afterwards (debrief).

los.text: Distinguish between various types of back pain (e.g., musculoskeletal, neuropathic, visceral) and recognise their unique clinical presentations
los.html:
TypeFeatures
Mechanical / non-specific (musculoskeletal)Commonest (~90%); lumbosacral, worse with movement and loading, eased by rest; no neurological deficit
Radicular (neuropathic)
  • Sciatica: sharp, shooting or burning pain below the knee in a dermatomal pattern (L5, S1), pins and needles, worse on coughing
  • Usually disc prolapse
Spinal stenosisNeurogenic claudication: leg pain on walking/standing, eased by sitting or bending forward; older patients
Inflammatory (axial spondyloarthritis)Onset <40, insidious, >3 months, morning stiffness >30 min, better with exercise, worse with rest, night pain (second half), alternating buttock pain
Visceral / referredNot affected by movement; systemic features: AAA (pulsatile mass, shock), renal colic, pyelonephritis, pancreatitis, posterior peptic ulcer, gynaecological
Serious spinal pathology
  • Cancer (history of cancer, weight loss, night pain)
  • Infection (fever, IVDU, immunosuppression: discitis, epidural abscess)
  • Fracture (osteoporosis, steroids, trauma)
  • Cauda equina (saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel disturbance, bilateral sciatica)

los.text: Identify and list key differences in physical examination findings for different types of back pain
los.html:
TypeExamination findings
MechanicalParaspinal tenderness and spasm, reduced and painful range, normal neurology, negative SLR
Radicular
  • Positive straight leg raise (L5/S1, 30–70°) or femoral stretch test (L2–4)
  • Dermatomal sensory loss
  • Myotomal weakness (L5: big toe extension, S1: plantarflexion)
  • Reduced ankle jerk (S1) or knee jerk (L4)
InflammatoryReduced lumbar flexion (Schober's test), sacroiliac tenderness, reduced chest expansion, enthesitis, uveitis, psoriasis
VisceralNormal spine movement; abdominal signs (pulsatile expansile mass, renal angle tenderness, epigastric tenderness)
Cauda equinaSaddle anaesthesia, reduced anal tone, bilateral leg signs, palpable bladder (retention)
Cord compressionUMN signs (increased tone, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars), sensory level
Malignancy / infection / fractureFocal bony tenderness, fever, weight loss, kyphosis

los.text: Apply examination findings and clinical reasoning to select appropriate interventional pathways, including conservative, medical, or surgical options
los.html:
FindingPathway
Non-specific low back pain (NICE NG59)
  • Conservative: reassurance, stay active, exercise programmes, manual therapy only alongside exercise, psychological therapy (CBT) combined with exercise
  • NSAID (lowest dose, shortest time, PPI if needed)
  • Weak opioid only short term if NSAIDs unsuitable
  • No paracetamol alone, no routine imaging
  • STarT Back to target intensity
Sciatica
  • As above
  • No gabapentinoids, other antiepileptics, oral steroids or benzodiazepines (NICE)
  • Epidural steroid injection for acute severe sciatica
  • Spinal decompression (discectomy) if persistent despite conservative care with concordant MRI
Chronic facet-type painRadiofrequency denervation after a positive diagnostic medial branch block
Spinal stenosisPhysio, analgesia; decompression for severe neurogenic claudication
Cauda equinaEmergency MRI and surgical decompression
Suspected cancer, infection, fractureUrgent imaging (MRI), bloods (FBC, CRP, ESR, calcium, myeloma screen, PSA), oncology/orthopaedic referral
InflammatoryRheumatology referral: HLA-B27, MRI sacroiliac joints; NSAIDs, physiotherapy, biologics (anti-TNF)
VisceralTreat the cause (e.g. CT for AAA → vascular surgery)

los.text: Describe the legal classification of controlled drugs.
los.html:
Misuse of Drugs Act 1971Classifies drugs as Class A, B or C by harm, setting criminal penalties for possession and supply (e.g. A: heroin, cocaine, morphine; B: cannabis, ketamine, codeine; C: benzodiazepines, tramadol, gabapentinoids, anabolic steroids).
Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001Schedules 1–5 govern legitimate use (prescribing, storage, records):
ScheduleExamplesMain controls
1LSD, MDMA, raw cannabisNo therapeutic use; Home Office licence
2Morphine, diamorphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, methadone, amphetamines, cocaine, ketamineFull CD prescription requirements, safe custody (locked CD cupboard), CD register, witnessed destruction
3Buprenorphine, tramadol, midazolam, temazepam, gabapentin, pregabalin, phenobarbitalPrescription requirements; safe custody for some (e.g. buprenorphine, temazepam); no register
4Benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam), zopiclone; anabolic steroidsStandard prescription; 28-day validity
5Low-strength preparations (co-codamol, codeine tablets, oral morphine 10 mg/5 mL)Few controls (invoices kept)

los.text: Prescribe controlled drugs on inpatient prescriptions and for discharge in accordance with current legal prescription requirements.
los.html:
• Prescription requirements for Schedule 2 and 3 CDs (outpatient and discharge/TTO prescriptions):
1Patient's full name and address (age if under 12).
2Drug name, form (e.g. tablets, MR capsules) and strength (if more than one exists).
3Dose (clear: "as directed" isn't acceptable; "one tablet twice a day" is).
4Total quantity or number of dose units in both words and figures (e.g. "twenty-eight (28) tablets").
5Prescriber's signature (indelible), date, and address.
Good practiceMaximum 30 days' supply; prescription valid for 28 days; state the brand for MR opioids (e.g. "Zomorph"), never ambiguous abbreviations.
Inpatient chart
  • Standard chart rules (approved name, dose, route, frequency, start date, signature)
  • PRN entries need the indication, minimum interval and maximum in 24 hours
  • Ward CD stock is recorded in the CD register with two signatures.
Example discharge"Morphine sulfate MR tablets (Zomorph) 10 mg: 10 mg twice daily. Supply: fourteen (14) tablets."

los.text: Convert between different opioids.
los.html:
• Use oral morphine as the reference
    • divide or multiply by the conversion factor
    • reduce by 25–50% when switching to a different opioid (incomplete cross-tolerance)
    • round down
    • prescribe breakthrough doses
    • review closely.
From → toConversion
Oral codeine → oral morphine÷ 10 (codeine 240 mg/day ≈ morphine 24 mg/day)
Oral tramadol → oral morphine÷ 10 (BNF)
Oral morphine → oral oxycodone÷ 1.5 to 2 (oxycodone is more potent; check local guidance)
Oral morphine → SC morphine÷ 2
Oral morphine → SC diamorphine÷ 3
Oral oxycodone → SC oxycodone÷ 1.5 to 2
Fentanyl 12 micrograms/h patch≈ 30–45 mg/day oral morphine (25 micrograms/h ≈ 60–90 mg/day)
Buprenorphine 5 micrograms/h patch≈ 12 mg/day oral morphine
  • Worked example: MR morphine 30 mg twice daily = 60 mg/24 h oral → SC morphine 30 mg/24 h via syringe driver
    • breakthrough = 1/6 of 30 = 5 mg SC PRN (oral breakthrough before = 10 mg).
  • Patches are for stable pain (slow onset and offset, ~12–24 h); not for acute titration.

los.text: Prescribe on a syringe driver chart.
los.html:
• Continuous subcutaneous infusion (CSCI) over 24 hours when oral route is unsuitable (dysphagia, vomiting, bowel obstruction, last days, poor absorption).
On the syringe driver chart
Each drug: approved name, total dose over 24 h (e.g. "Morphine sulfate 30 mg/24 h")
Diluent: usually water for injections (cyclizine precipitates in sodium chloride)
Compatibility of combined drugs (check a syringe driver compatibility guide, e.g. Palliative Care Formulary; usually up to 3 drugs)
Route SC, start date and time, signature; syringe volume and rate set per local device (e.g. T34)
Separate PRN SC doses for breakthrough pain (1/6 of the 24-h opioid dose), nausea, agitation and secretions
Typical drugsMorphine/oxycodone/alfentanil (pain), levomepromazine/haloperidol/cyclizine (nausea), midazolam (agitation), hyoscine butylbromide (secretions).
Practicalities
  • Start when the next oral MR dose is due (give a PRN if needed meanwhile)
  • Check the site (redness, swelling) and running every 4 hours
  • a fentanyl patch is usually left on and the driver added for extra needs.

los.text: Elicit a focused falls history, and identify common causes of falls in older adults.
sessions: History of falls and Osteoporosis explaining
los.html:
Falls history
Before: what were you doing? Warning symptoms: dizziness on standing (postural hypotension), palpitations, chest pain, vertigo, sudden weakness
During: loss of consciousness (syncope vs seizure), witnessed account (jerking, colour, duration), tongue biting, incontinence
After: injuries, confusion, "long lie" (unable to get up: rhabdomyolysis, pressure damage, hypothermia, pneumonia)
Background: previous falls, fear of falling, mobility and aids, vision, hearing, continence (rushing to the toilet, nocturia), cognition, mood
Medications: antihypertensives, diuretics, sedatives (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs), antidepressants, antipsychotics, opioids, hypoglycaemics, anticholinergics; polypharmacy
Social: alcohol, home hazards (stairs, rugs, lighting), footwear, support, carers
  • Common causes: usually multifactorial: muscle weakness and gait/balance problems
    • postural hypotension
    • drugs
    • visual impairment
    • cognitive impairment
    • cardiac syncope (arrhythmia, aortic stenosis)
    • Parkinson's disease
    • stroke
    • peripheral neuropathy
    • arthritis and foot problems
    • acute illness (infection, delirium)
    • environment.

los.text: Describe appropriate investigations to determine underlying causes
sessions: History of falls and Osteoporosis explaining
los.html:
InvestigationLooks for
Lying and standing BPPostural hypotension (systolic fall ≥20 mmHg or diastolic ≥10 mmHg within 3 minutes)
ECG (± 24-h tape, echo if murmur)Arrhythmia, heart block, long QT; aortic stenosis
Bloods: FBC, U&E, glucose, TFTs, calcium, B12/folate, CK (long lie), vitamin DAnaemia, dehydration, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, rhabdomyolysis
Urine dip (only if symptomatic) and infection screenAcute illness
Medication review (STOPP/START)Drugs causing falls
Gait and balance: Timed Up and Go (≥12 s = high risk), Turn 180Mobility
Vision, feet, cognition (4AT, AMTS)Contributors
Imaging for injuriesX-ray (hip, wrist); CT head if head injury and on anticoagulants or other NICE criteria
Bone health: FRAX/QFracture ± DEXAOsteoporosis
  • Leads to a multifactorial falls risk assessment and intervention: strength and balance training
    • home hazard assessment (OT)
    • medication changes
    • vision correction
    • treat postural hypotension.

los.text: Explain the pathophysiology, risk factors, and consequences of osteoporosis, and describe evidence-based prevention and treatment options in a way any patient can understand
sessions: History of falls and Osteoporosis explaining
los.html:
What it is
  • Bones lose density and quality, so they break easily (fragility fractures: from standing height or less). "Your bones have become thinner and more fragile, like a honeycomb with bigger holes.
  • It doesn't hurt by itself, but it means a fall is more likely to cause a break."
Pathophysiology
  • Bone is constantly remodelled
  • Osteoclast resorption exceeds osteoblast formation.
  • Oestrogen loss at menopause increases RANKL → more osteoclasts
  • Peak bone mass by ~30, then gradual loss.
DiagnosisDEXA T-score ≤ −2.5 (osteopenia −1 to −2.5); 10-year fracture risk with FRAX or QFracture.
Risk factors
Age, female sex, early menopause, low BMI (<18.5), previous fragility fracture, parental hip fracture
Smoking, alcohol >3 units/day, inactivity
Glucocorticoids (≥3 months), aromatase inhibitors, antiepileptics, PPIs (weak)
RA, hyperthyroidism, hypogonadism, malabsorption (coeliac), CKD, diabetes
Consequences
  • Hip, vertebral and wrist fractures
  • Pain, kyphosis and height loss
  • Loss of independence
  • ~1 in 4–5 die within a year of a hip fracture.
PreventionWeight-bearing and resistance exercise, calcium (700–1200 mg/day) and vitamin D (800–1000 IU/day), stop smoking, limit alcohol, falls prevention.
TreatmentKey points
Oral bisphosphonate (alendronic acid 70 mg weekly, risedronate)
  • First line
  • Take first thing on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, stay upright 30 min
  • SEs: oesophagitis, rare osteonecrosis of the jaw (dental check), atypical femoral fracture
  • Review after 5 years
IV zoledronic acid (yearly)If oral not tolerated
Denosumab (6-monthly SC, anti-RANKL)Check calcium; don't stop suddenly (rebound vertebral fractures)
Teriparatide (daily PTH analogue), romosozumabAnabolic; severe/multiple vertebral fractures
HRT / raloxifeneYounger postmenopausal women

los.text: Identify in detail the nerves that carry cutaneous innervation of the skin of the face and scalp.
los.html:
RegionNerveDivision
Forehead, upper eyelid, scalp to the vertexSupraorbital, supratrochlearV1 (frontal nerve)
Side and tip of nose (dorsum)Infratrochlear, external nasalV1 (nasociliary)
Lower eyelid, cheek, side of nose, upper lipInfraorbitalV2
Over the zygoma / anterior templeZygomaticofacial, zygomaticotemporalV2
Lower lip, chinMentalV3 (inferior alveolar)
Cheek over the buccinatorBuccalV3
Temple, front of the earAuriculotemporalV3
Angle of the jaw, parotid area, lower earGreat auricular (C2–3)Cervical plexus, not trigeminal
Back of the scalpGreater occipital (C2), lesser occipital (C2), third occipital (C3)Posterior/anterior rami
  • Clinical: the angle of the mandible is spared in trigeminal lesions (C2–3).
    • Shingles follows one division
    • trigeminal neuralgia is usually V2 or V3.
    • Supraorbital, infraorbital and mental foramina lie on one vertical line (nerve blocks).

los.text: Explain that the face has no deep fascia, only superficial fascia.
los.html:
• No deep fascia in the face: the muscles of expression lie in the superficial fascia, attached to skin.
  • Why it matters:
ConsequenceDetail
Muscles move skinFine facial expression
Swelling spreads easilyLoose tissue: eyelids swell a lot (allergy, trauma, nephrotic syndrome); bruising tracks
Wounds gapeMuscle pull opens lacerations; repair in layers
Infection spreadsNo fascial barrier, so cellulitis spreads freely
  • Exception: the parotid is wrapped in a tough parotid fascia (from the investing layer), so parotitis is very painful.

los.text: Recognise the extracranial courses of the branches of the facial nerve.
los.html:
• Exit: stylomastoid foramen
    • → gives posterior auricular nerve and branches to the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid
    • → enters the parotid gland
    • → divides (pes anserinus) superficial to the retromandibular vein and external carotid artery into five branches.
BranchCourseSupplies
TemporalCrosses the zygomatic archFrontalis, upper orbicularis oculi
ZygomaticAlong the zygomatic arch to the lateral eyeOrbicularis oculi (eye closure)
BuccalAcross the masseter with the parotid ductBuccinator, upper lip muscles
Marginal mandibularAlong the lower border of the mandible (can dip below it)Lower lip depressors
CervicalDown into the neckPlatysma
  • Mnemonic: "To Zanzibar By Motor Car".

los.text: Link the muscles of facial expression to each branch of the facial nerve and describe the consequences of injury to each branch
los.html:
BranchKey musclesInjury
TemporalFrontalis, corrugatorCan't raise the eyebrow; brow droops (e.g. temple surgery, forehead lacerations)
ZygomaticOrbicularis oculiCan't close the eye fully → exposure keratitis
BuccalBuccinator, zygomaticus, orbicularis oris (upper)Food collects in the cheek; weak smile
Marginal mandibularDepressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, mentalisAsymmetric lower lip when smiling (submandibular gland surgery, neck incisions)
CervicalPlatysmaLittle functional loss
  • Whole nerve (LMN, e.g. Bell's palsy): whole half of the face, including the forehead.
    • UMN (stroke): forehead spared (bilateral cortical supply to the upper face).

los.text: Name the facial muscles of expression as either sphincters or dilators by describing their actions (and innervations).
los.html:
GroupMuscleActionNerve
SphinctersOrbicularis oculiCloses the eye (gentle: palpebral; tight: orbital part)Temporal, zygomatic
Orbicularis orisCloses and purses the lipsBuccal, marginal mandibular
Compressor narisNarrows the nostrilBuccal
DilatorsLevator labii superioris, zygomaticus major and minorRaise the lip, smileZygomatic, buccal
Depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferiorisLower the mouth corner and lipMarginal mandibular
Dilator narisWidens the nostrilBuccal
Frontalis, corrugator superciliiRaise the brow / frownTemporal
OthersBuccinatorKeeps food between the teeth, blowingBuccal
PlatysmaTenses neck skin, lowers the mandibleCervical
  • All are supplied by the facial nerve (2nd pharyngeal arch); muscles of mastication are V3 (1st arch).

los.text: Describe the intracranial and intrapetrous course of the facial nerve and the relationships of its major branches to the middle ear in relation to damage of the nerve within the facial canal.
los.html:
1. IntracranialLeaves the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle with VIII (motor root + nervus intermedius) → internal acoustic meatus.
2. Labyrinthine segment(narrowest part of the facial canal)Geniculate ganglion: gives the greater petrosal nerve (lacrimal gland, nasal and palatal glands).
3. Tympanic segment
  • Runs horizontally on the medial wall of the middle ear, above the oval window
  • Its bony covering can be thin or missing → spread of otitis media, injury in middle ear surgery.
4. Mastoid segment
  • Turns down behind the middle ear
  • Gives the nerve to stapedius then the chorda tympani (crosses the inner eardrum between the malleus and incus).
5Exits at the stylomastoid foramen.
Lesion levelExtra features beyond facial weakness
Above the geniculate ganglionDry eye, hyperacusis, lost taste
Between ganglion and stapedius nerveHyperacusis, lost taste (tears normal)
Between stapedius and chorda tympaniLost taste on the anterior 2/3 of the tongue
Below the chorda tympani (stylomastoid / parotid)Facial weakness only
  • Ramsay Hunt syndrome: VZV at the geniculate ganglion: vesicles in the ear canal, facial palsy, ± deafness and vertigo.

los.text: Describe the origin, functions and major branches of the sensory and motor components of the facial nerve.
los.html:
ComponentFibresRouteFunction
Branchial motorFacial motor nucleus (pons)Main trunk → 5 branches; stapedius, posterior digastric, stylohyoidFacial expression, damps loud sound
ParasympatheticSuperior salivatory nucleusGreater petrosal → pterygopalatine ganglionLacrimal, nasal and palatal glands
Chorda tympani → lingual nerve → submandibular ganglionSubmandibular and sublingual glands
Special sense (taste)Nucleus of the solitary tractChorda tympani (and greater petrosal for the palate)Taste, anterior 2/3 of tongue
General sensationSpinal trigeminal nucleusSmall branchSkin of the concha and ear canal
  • Nervus intermedius: the sensory and parasympathetic root.
    • The parotid gland is supplied by IX (via the otic ganglion), not VII, even though VII runs through it.

los.text: Describe the facial artery and transverse facial artery, their origins and courses.
los.html:
ArteryOriginCourseClinical
Facial arteryECA (just above the lingual, often a common trunk)
  • Deep to the posterior digastric and stylohyoid
  • → grooves the submandibular gland
  • → hooks over the lower border of the mandible at the front of masseter (pulse here)
  • → tortuous course past the angle of the mouth (superior and inferior labial branches)
  • → angular artery at the medial eye
Lip lacerations bleed briskly from both sides (labial arteries anastomose)
Transverse facial arterySuperficial temporal artery (inside the parotid)Forward across the masseter, above the parotid duct, below the zygomatic archSupplies the parotid, its duct and masseter
  • Rich anastomoses across the midline and with ICA branches (angular–ophthalmic), so facial wounds bleed freely but heal well.

los.text: Describe the facial veins and their tributaries, explaining the risks of the spread of infection intracranially
los.html:
Facial vein
  • Begins as the angular vein at the medial eye
  • → runs down behind the facial artery (straighter)
  • → crosses the mandible
  • → joins the anterior division of the retromandibular vein
  • → internal jugular vein.
TributariesSupraorbital and supratrochlear veins, labial veins, deep facial vein (from the pterygoid plexus).
Route to the brainPath
Superior ophthalmic veinAngular vein → superior ophthalmic vein → cavernous sinus
Deep facial veinFacial vein → pterygoid plexus → emissary veins → cavernous sinus
Why infection spreadsThe veins have few or no valves, so blood can flow backwards when the face is swollen.
"Danger triangle"Corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose: squeezing spots or infections here can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis (proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, fever).

los.text: Describe the relationship of the termination of the facial vein (draining into the internal jugular vein) and the mandibular branch of the retromandibular vein (draining facial muscles controlling the angle of the mouth) to the submandibular gland and related upper jugular lymph nodes in relation to exploration of this area.
los.html:
Facial vein termination
  • Crosses the superficial surface of the submandibular gland, joined by the anterior division of the retromandibular vein, then drains into the IJV near the level of the hyoid
  • The upper jugular (jugulodigastric) nodes lie here.
Marginal mandibular nerveRuns deep to platysma but superficial to the facial vein and artery, along or up to ~2 cm below the mandible.
In practice(submandibular gland excision, node biopsy, neck dissection)
StepReason
Incise 2–3 finger-breadths below the mandibleAvoids the marginal mandibular nerve
Tie the facial vein low and reflect it upwards (Hayes Martin manoeuvre)Lifts the nerve, lying on the vein, out of harm's way
Expect upper jugular nodes beside the vein and glandCommon sites of metastases
  • Injury: weak depressor anguli oris → drooping lower lip on smiling.

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the scalp, naming its individual layers.
los.html:
Layer (SCALP)DetailClinical
SkinThick, hairy, many sebaceous glandsSebaceous cysts
Connective tissue (dense)Fibrous septa hold the vessels, which can't retractProfuse bleeding from cuts
Aponeurosis (epicranial)Galea joining occipitofrontalis belliesWounds through it gape
Loose areolar tissueAllows the scalp to move; emissary veins cross it"Danger layer": blood and pus spread here and infection reaches the dural sinuses; subgaleal haemorrhage in neonates
PericraniumPeriosteum of the skull, attached at suturesCephalohaematoma stays within one bone
  • Scalping injuries separate through the loose areolar layer.

los.text: Describe the blood supply of the scalp and its significance in laceration injuries.
los.html:
Arteries (from front to back)Origin
Supratrochlear, supraorbitalICA (ophthalmic artery)
Superficial temporalECA
Posterior auricularECA
OccipitalECA
AnastomosesRich, across the midline and between ICA and ECA territories, so a scalp flap survives on a narrow pedicle.
Lacerations bleed heavily
  • Vessels are held open by the dense connective tissue and can't contract
  • Control with pressure, then suture through the dense layer (or haemostatic clips).
Veins follow the arteries; emissary veins link them to the dural sinuses.
LymphFront of the scalp to parotid nodes, back to mastoid and occipital nodes.

los.text: Locate the occipitofrontalis muscle and describe its actions.
los.html:
OccipitofrontalisTwo frontal bellies (no bony origin: blend with the skin of the eyebrows) and two occipital bellies (superior nuchal line), joined by the epicranial aponeurosis (galea).
Actions
  • Frontal belly raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead (surprise)
  • Occipital belly pulls the scalp back
  • Together they move the scalp.
NerveFacial nerve (temporal branch to frontalis, posterior auricular branch to occipitalis).
Testing"raise your eyebrows": preserved in a UMN facial palsy, lost in a LMN palsy.

los.text: Trace the path and distribution of the maxillary artery and its main branches in the infratemporal fossa.
los.html:
• Maxillary artery: larger terminal branch of the ECA, starts behind the neck of the mandible in the parotid
    • → through the infratemporal fossa (superficial or deep to the lateral pterygoid)
    • → enters the pterygopalatine fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure.
PartMain branchesSupply
1st (mandibular), behind the mandibular neckMiddle meningeal (through foramen spinosum), inferior alveolar (mandibular foramen), deep auricular, anterior tympanicDura and skull; lower teeth, chin
2nd (pterygoid), on the lateral pterygoidDeep temporal, masseteric, pterygoid, buccalMuscles of mastication
3rd (pterygopalatine)Posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, descending palatine, sphenopalatineUpper teeth, face, palate, nasal cavity (posterior epistaxis)
  • Clinical: middle meningeal → extradural haematoma; sphenopalatine → posterior nosebleeds (ligated endoscopically).

los.text: Describe the pterygoid venous plexus.
los.html:
• Pterygoid venous plexus: network around the lateral pterygoid in the infratemporal fossa
    • drains the territory of the maxillary artery and empties into the maxillary vein (→ retromandibular vein).
ConnectionSignificance
Deep facial vein → facial veinFacial infection can reach the plexus
Emissary veins (foramen ovale, foramen lacerum) → cavernous sinusRoute for spread of infection intracranially
Inferior ophthalmic veinOrbital link
FunctionActs as a pump: chewing squeezes blood out of it.
Clinical
  • a posterior superior alveolar nerve block can puncture it → haematoma in the cheek
  • Dental and facial infections → cavernous sinus thrombosis.

los.text: Recognise structures of the face on radiographic images.
los.html:
• Plain films: occipitomental (OM) views (15° and 30°) show the orbits
    • maxillary sinuses
    • zygomatic arches and nasal bones: check the "elephant's head" outline of the zygoma
    • orbital margins and the dental lines (McGrigor's lines).
FindingSuggests
Fluid level in a maxillary sinus after traumaFracture (blood in the sinus)
"Teardrop" soft tissue hanging from the orbital roof into the maxillary sinusOrbital floor blowout fracture
Step in the orbital rim or zygomatic archZygomatic (tripod) fracture
Fluid level or opacified sinus without traumaSinusitis
  • Orthopantomogram (OPG): mandible, teeth, condyles (mandibular fractures).
  • CT is now standard for facial fractures (Le Fort I, II, III patterns).
